question:
Crew Management (Training)
If the vessel is equipped with an Electronic Chart Display and Information System （ECDIS）, as stated on the Form E of the SEC,  have the Master and Deck officers’ complete Generic and type specific familiarization on the system fitted onboard?
Is ECDIS on board familiarization has been undertaken?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check by asking Master, officers.

If SAFEQUIP Cert Form "E" shows ECDIS as primary means of navigation, then all deck officers MUST be in possession of Generic (IMO Model course 1.27)
Check if Master has issued instructions for minimum safety settings (Alarm) for following
i)           Cross Track Error
ii)          Safety Depth
iii)        Safety Contour
iv)        Shallow and Deep Contour
and how are these being adhered to by OOWs.
<Annotation>
Type specific training is not mandatory, but required for RIGHTSHIP inspection.
Notes: ECDIS phase in started on 1st July 2012 for new tankers, 1st July 2015 existing tankers. If ECDIS is fitted, either single ECDIS or duplicate for redundancy purposes and being used for navigation but paper charts are retained as the primary source of navigation, then all watch keeping officers must have both generic training and type specific familiarization as accepted  by the vessels flag. (Type specific familiarization is not required if the Generic training was conducted on the same unit as fitted on board).
If the vessel is fitted with an ECDIS system that is not fully compliant with respect to redundancy etc. and the primary source of navigation is paper charts, then all watchkeeping officers must have generic training.
Each deck watchkeeper must be in possession of an ECDIS Generic Training certificate. This Generic training must have taken place at an establishment approved by the Flag Administration, address the subjects set out in, and fully address each of the topics contained in the IMO Model Course 1.27, (The operational use of Electronic Chart Display and Information Systems （ECDIS）). An ECDIS Generic Training Certificate conducted on the 2010 syllabus is acceptable.
If the equipment on board is of a different type (manufacturer) to which the generic training was undertaken, then evidence of familiarization of the actual equipment fitted on board should
be provided. The document "ECDIS - Industry Recommendations for ECDIS Familiarization" (Published by the Nautical Institute) or an equivalent produced by the manager should be completed to demonstrate such familiarization. Record in comments the nature of and duration of such familiarization. If only one ECDIS fitted and paper charts are also provided record which is the primary source of navigation and which is the backup.

For example: donning of immersion suits, starting L/B engine etc.
<Annotation>
Instructions in the use of the ship’s fire extinguishing appliances, life-saving appliances and in survival at sea shall be given at the same interval as the drills. Individual instruction may cover different parts of the ship’s life-saving and fire-extinguishing appliances, but all shall be covered within any period of two months. (SOLAS III/19.4.1)
Every crew member shall be given instructions which shall include but not necessarily be limited to:
1. Operation and use of the ship’s inflatable life rafts;
2. Problems of hypothermia, first-aid treatment for hypothermia and other appropriate first-aid procedures;
3. Special instructions necessary for use of the ship’s life-saving appliances in severe weather and severe sea conditions; and,
4. Operation and use of fire-extinguishing appliances. (SOLAS III/19.4.2)
As far as is reasonable and practicable, rescue boats other than lifeboats which are also rescue boats, shall be launched each month with their assigned crew aboard and maneuvered in the water. In all cases this requirement shall be complied with at least every three months. (SOLAS III/19.3.3.6)

question:
Crew Management (Fatigue Control)
Are the STCW and flag Administration’s regulations that control hours of work to minimize fatigue being followed?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check the requirements with DMLC Part II. Check HRM S 521 Shipboard Working arrangement.
Check HRM S 520 Work Rest Hour record for officers and ratings
<Annotation>
Records should be kept for the Master, officers and all other members of the ships compliment to the specific ILO format.
However, the basis for calculating hours of rest should be demonstrated as being consistent with the Conventions’ requirements and, where applicable, with the interpretations of the OCIMF paper. OCIMF require that the term ‘any 24 hours’ is interpreted and applied literally and is not linked to calendar days or a fixed time of starting work or rest.
It should be ensured that, at any time during the working period, in the past 24 hours the seafarer should always be in compliance with the requirements for a minimum of 10 hours rest which has been divided into no more than 2 periods, one of which is to be a minimum of 6 hours.
The ILO format “Working Hours Record” contains columns for:
- “Hours of rest in 24 hour period”
- “Hours of Rest in any 24 hour period” A figure of less than 10 in this column indicates a day when non-conformance has occurred.
- A third column should indicate the “Hours of rest in any 7 day period” A figure of less than 77 in this column indicates a non-conformance has occurred.   Inspectors should observe if the records are not to ILO format or have columns that have not been completed unless another method of confirming conformance is available.
Although the regulations only require monitoring of hours to be undertaken on board, it is important that managers ashore have access to meaningful summary data that enables them to monitor the work and rest hours of individuals.
The Inspector should record an observation:
- If “any 24 hours” is not interpreted literally, or
- a lack of evidence of conformance/non-conformance calculations, or
- any lack of evidence that managers are informed at least monthly of compliance levels on board, or
- a failure by the manager to acknowledge significant levels of non-conformance (3 or more days containing “non-conformance” by any individual on board)

question:
Safety Management (Document Control)
Do the company’s procedures manuals comply with ISM Code requirements?
guideline:
<Check point>
<Annotation>
The Company should ensure that the safety management system operating on board the ship contains a clear statement emphasizing the Master’s authority. The Company should establish in the safety management system that the Master has the overriding authority and the responsibility to make decisions with respect to safety and pollution prevention and to request the Company’s assistance as may be necessary. (ISM Code 5.2)
Notes: It is not a requirement that the manuals be written in English. However, if not, the fact should be recorded in Comments. Key elements of the ISM Code that should be incorporated into the procedures manuals are that they should be:
- Relevant to the ship;
- User friendly;
- Written in the working language of the crew. And that they should at least contain:
- A safety and environmental policy;
- Emergency procedures;
Emergency procedures should at least include collision, grounding, flooding, heavy weather damage, structural failure, fire (on deck and in cargo tanks, the engine room, pump room and accommodation), explosion, gas or toxic vapor release, critical machinery failure, rescue from enclosed spaces, serious injury and helicopter operations.
- A description of the Master’s and crew’s responsibilities;
- Shipboard operation plans;
- Procedures for reporting non-conformities and for corrective action;
- Maintenance programmes;
- Procedures for auditing and reviews;
- Programmed of drills,
The programmed of drills must at least include the emergency procedures detailed above and in addition abandon ship, man overboard, pollution clean-up and ship security including dealing with terrorism and piracy.
Occasionally the company’s procedures are available only in computerized versions. Ascertain whether there is adequate access for all personnel to a computer and whether adequate training has been given to all personnel in accessing the company’s procedures using one. In any case, an up to date copy of the company’s navigation policy and procedures must be available on the bridge and officers should demonstrate familiarity with the policy. If the policy is provided in electronic format only, a back-up independent means of power supply to the computer must be provided.

question:
Safety Management (Document Control)
Are Cyber Security Policy and Cyber security procedures as per Cyber Security Manual?
guideline:
<Check point>
check cyber security policy

The cyber security management shall:
• Who is the SCSO of the vessel?;
Can vessel staff identify CCSO?
• Is the ship specific risk assessment available onboard  ;
• Implement technical measures to protect against a cyber-incident and ensure continuity of operations. This may include configuration of networks, access control to networks and systems, communication and boundary defence and the use of protection and detection software;
• Implement activities and plans (procedural protection measures) to provide resilience against cyber incidents. This may include training and awareness, software maintenance, remote and local access, access privileges, use of removable media and equipment disposal
• Implement activities to prepare for and respond to cyber incidents.
Note: Do the procedures include a risk assessment of issues such as:
• Threats such as from malware; phishing attacks etc.
• Identification and protection of Vulnerable systems (ECDIS etc)
• Mitigation measures, (USB control etc)
• Identify key personnel within the company (including who the master reports suspected incidents to)
• Hard copy of key contacts (e.g. DPA; CSO etc).
• Password management/record?
• Contractor compliance
Note: Does the Cyber Response plan contain guidance on:
• What ‘symptoms’ to look for,
• Immediate actions to be taken and
• Name, position, phone number and email for the Responsible Person to be contacted

question:
Safety Management (Internal Audit)
Is a recent company’s internal audit report available and is a close-out system in place for dealing with non-conformities?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check SQE F 602 Internal Audit Report. Check if all observations are closed out with final comments from company. Note last date of I.A.
Check for CARs and other Company's document which shows that correction has been complete.
Pick out randomly some nonconformities found in internal audit, and check to see if those have been corrected.
<Annotation>
Note: This audit must be conducted as part of the company’s SMS procedures. Satisfactory evidence should record that corrective action was taken to rectify non-conformities. A close-out system, which includes a time limit for corrective action, informing the company when completed and the company ensuring that it has been, should be in place and the inspector should ensure that the required actions have been made within the required time. Inspectors must not use company’s audits as a means to record Finding. Some administrations may permit an extension for this review.

question:
Bridge Management (General)
Are the deck officers’ familiar with the operators Under Keel Clearance policy, able to demonstrate satisfactory UKC and squat calculations for the last voyage and is the policy comprehensive?
Is UKC calculated and written for each leg of the Passage Plan?
Is company policy relating to underkeel clearance included as part of the Master/Pilot exchange in the form of a written underkeel calculation?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check SPM N 127- Passage Plan (ECDIS Vessels) & SPM N 128- Squat Calculation

Check the block coefficient used for the calculation of squat is correct UKC calculations shall consider squat, tidal conditions, sea bottom, reliability of hydrographic data,  CATZOC, etc.
<Annotation>
Record in Comments, the company’s policy relating to under keel clearance requirements for ocean passage, shallow water, within port limits and while alongside the berth or at SBM/CBM
mooring.
Note: The company's policy relating to under keel clearance should be included as part of the Master/Pilot interchange in the form of a written under keel calculation. The policy must
provide a minimum allowed under keel clearance for both coastal, river navigation, while alongside and guidance on the action to be taken in shallow water to ensure the minimum clearance
is maintained.
Under keel clearance can be affected by several factors and the under keel calculations should include, but not necessarily be limited to;
 - The predicted height of the tide;
 - Changes in the predicted tidal height, which are caused by wind speed and direction and high or low barometric pressure;
 - Nature and stability of the bottom – i.e. sand waves, siltation etc.;
 - Accuracy of hydrographic data,  (References to reliability is often included on charts);
 - Change of water density and the increase in draught due to fresh water allowance;
 - The vessel’s size and handling characteristics and increase in draught due to heel;
 - Wave response allowance, which is the vertical displacement of the hull due to heave, roll and pitch motions;
 - The reliability of draft observations and calculations, including estimates of hogging and sagging;
 - Reduced depths over pipelines and other obstructions.
Accuracy of hydrographic data, (References to reliability is often included on charts or in the form of CATZOC on ENC's)* ;
*consideration of the CATZOC should be captured within the UKC calculation or policy.

question:
Bridge Management (Watchkeeping)
Has the Bridge been adequately manned at all stages of the voyage and at Anchor and were lookout arrangement adequate?
Is a  systematic lookout maintained using combination of methods (visual check using the naked eyes or binocular, RADAR/ARPA, hearing, etc.).
Are conditions under which Master must be called available?
Is Anchor Watch Checklist (ship's position, weather etc.) used?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check SMS Manuals and/or instructions in writing from Company.
Watch level on bridge shall be consistent with various conditions viz. traffic concentration, other navigational hazards, weather, visibility,
Day/ Night and with due regards to fatigue control of Bridge team members.
Bridge shall always be manned at Anchorage. Check if Master carried out thorough R.A. prior deciding One man watch on Bridge.
<Annotation>
Every vessel shall at all times maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing as well as by all available means appropriate to the prevailing circumstances and conditions as to make a full appraisal of the situation and the risk of collision. (Colregs Rule 5)
The look-out must be able to give his full attention to the keeping of a proper look-out and no other duties shall be undertaken or assigned which could interfere with that task. (STCW A-VIII/2-3.1/14)(STCW A-VIII/2-3.1/14)
The officer in charge of the navigational watch may be the sole look-out in daylight provided that on each occasion:
 - The situation has been carefully assessed and it has been established without doubt that it is safe to do so
 - Full account has been taken of all relevant factors including but not limited to:                                                                                                                                                                                                           o State of weather                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             o Visibility
o Traffic density
o Proximity of dangers to navigation; and
- The attention necessary when navigating in or near traffic separation schemes
- Assistance is immediately available to be summoned to the bridge when any change in the situation requires. (STCW A-VIII/2-3.1/15)
It is of special importance that at all times the officer in charge of the navigational watch ensures that a proper look-out is maintained. In a ship with a separate chartroom
the officer in charge of the navigational watch may visit the chartroom, when essential, for a short period for the necessary performance of navigational duties, but shall first
ensure that is safe to do so and that a proper look-out is maintained. (STCW A-VIII/2-3.1/32)
Note:
The company’s navigational instructions and procedures must contain guidance relating to circumstances when the officer of the watch may be the sole lookout including considerations that the OOW has had sufficient rest prior to starting the watch.
The experience of the watch officers, weather and traffic conditions will dictate the required bridge manning composition at any specific time. Each stage of the voyage must
be reviewed to establish that sufficient personnel were on the bridge and that an effective communications and teamwork structure was in place. Inspectors must take into
account the impact of additional bridge manning upon the work load of any individual and impact of hours of rest regulations.

<Annotation>
Muster lists and emergency instructions shall be exhibited in conspicuous places throughout the ship including the navigation bridge, engine room and crew accommodation spaces. (SOLAS III/8.3)
The muster list shall show the duties assigned to the different members of the crew including:
 - Closing of the watertight doors, fire doors, valves, scuppers, side scuttles, portholes and other similar openings in the ship;
 - Equipping of the survival craft and other life-saving appliances;
 - Preparation and launching of survival craft;
 - General preparations of other life-saving appliances;
 - Muster of passengers;
 - Use of communication equipment;
 - Manning of fire parties assigned to deal with fires; and
 - Special duties assigned in respect to the use of fire-fighting equipment and installations. (SOLAS III/37.3)
 - Illustrations and instructions in appropriate languages shall be posted in cabins and be conspicuously displayed at muster stations and other spaces to inform crew of:
 - their muster station;
 - the essential actions they must take in an emergency; and
 - the method of donning lifejackets.
The muster list shall specify which officers are assigned to ensure that life-saving and fire appliances are maintained in good condition and ready for immediate use.
(SOLAS III/37.4)

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Contingency Plan)
Are ship-specific life-saving equipment training manuals (SOLAS Trainig Manual) available?
guideline:
<Check point>
This manual shall be ship specific and free from generic instructions.
<Annotation>
A training manual shall be provided in each crew mess room and recreation room, or in each cabin. (SOLAS III/35.2)
The training manual shall contain instructions and information, in easily understood terms illustrated wherever possible, on the life-saving appliances
provided in the ship and on the best methods of survival. Any part of such information may be provided in the form of audio-visual aids in lieu of the manual.
The following shall be explained in detail:
 - Donning of lifejackets, immersion suits and anti-exposure suits;
 - Muster at assigned stations;
 - Boarding, launching and clearing the survival craft rescue boats; fast rescue boats, free-fall boats and inflated boats;
 - Method of launching from within survival craft;
 - Release from launching appliances;
 - methods and use of devices for protection in launching areas;
 - Illumination in launching areas;
 - Use of all survival equipment;
 - use of all detection equipment;
 - With the assistance of illustrations, the use of radio life-saving appliances;
 - Use of sea anchors
 - Use of engine and accessories;
 - Recovery of survival craft and rescue boats, fast rescue boats, free-fall boats and inflated boats including stowage and securing;
 - Hazards of exposure and the need for warm clothing;
 - Best use of survival craft facilities in order to survive;
 - Methods of retrieval, including the use of helicopter rescue gear; (slings, baskets, stretchers),breeches-buoy and shore life-saving apparatus and
ship’s line-throwing apparatus;
 - All other functions contained in the muster list and emergency instructions; and
 - Instructions for repair of the lifesaving appliances. (SOLAS III/35.3)

<Annotation>
The training manual shall explain the following in detail:
1. General fire safety practice and precautions related to the dangers of smoking, electrical hazards, flammable liquids and similar common shipboard hazards;
2. General instructions on fire-fighting activities and fire-fighting procedures, including procedures for notification of a fire and use of
manually operated call points;
3. Meanings of the ship’s alarms;
4. Operation and use of fire-fighting systems and appliances;
5. Operation and use of fire doors;
6. Operation and use of fire and smoke dampers; and
7. Escape systems and appliances. (SOLAS II-2/15.2.3.4)
A training manual shall be provided in each crew mess room and recreation room, or in each crew cabin. (SOLAS II-2/15.2.3.1)
The training manual shall be written in the working language of the ship. (SOLAS II-2/15.2.3.2)

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Drills)
Are abandon ship drill regularly held?
Are the crew familiar with their duties during lifeboat and are drills being performed effectively and on a frequency meeting SOLAS and flag state requirements?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check logbook or other records.
Check the on board evaluation record of drill for quality penetration amongst ship's crew
Check SEM S 800 Abandon Ship being utilized
<Annotation>
Every crew member shall participate in at least one abandon ship drill and one fire drill every month. The drills of the crew shall take place within 24 hours of the ship leaving a port if more than 25% of the crew have not participated in abandon ship and fire drills on board
that particular ship in the previous month. (SOLAS III/19.3.2)
Except as provided in paragraphs 3.3.4 and 3.3.5, each lifeboat shall be launched, and maneuvered in the water by its assigned operating crew, at least once every three months during an abandon ship drill.' (SOLAS III/19.3.3.3)
In the case of a lifeboat arranged for free-fall launching, at least once every three months during an abandon ship drill, the crew shall board the lifeboat, properly secure themselves in their seats and commence launch procedures up to, but not including, the actual release of the lifeboat (i.e., the release hook shall not be released). The lifeboat shall then either be free-fall launched with only the required operating crew on board, or lowered into the water by means of the secondary means of launching  without the operating crew on board. In both cases, the lifeboat shall thereafter be maneuvered in the water by the operating crew. At intervals of not more than six
months, the lifeboat shall either be launched by free fall with only the operating crew on board, or simulated launching shall be carried out in accordance with the guidelines developed by the Organization. (See MSC.1/Circ.1206/Rev.1) (SOLAS III/19.3.3.4) MSC.1/Circ.1578

The fire drill must be included at least the following matters.

 - Are procedure of engine room ventilation control established?
 - Are instruction and confirmation by command in the bridge available?

guideline:
<Check point>

<Annotation>
Every crew member shall participate in at least one abandon ship drill and one fire drill every month. The drills of the crew shall take place within 24 hours of the ship leaving a port if more than 25% of the crew have not participated in abandon ship and fire drills on board that particular ship in the previous month. (SOLAS III/19.3.2)
Fire drills should be planned in such a way that due consideration is given to regular practice in the various emergencies that may occur depending on the type of ship and the cargo. (SOLAS III/19.3.4.1)
Crew members shall be trained to be familiar with the arrangements of the ship as well as the location and operation of any fire-fighting systems and appliances that they may be called upon to use. (SOLAS 2004 II-2/15.2.2.1)
Each fire drill shall include:
1. Reporting to stations and preparing for the duties described in the muster list;
2. Starting a fire pump, using at least the two required jets of water to show that the system is in proper working order;
3. Checking of fireman’s outfit and other personal rescue equipment;
4. Checking of relevant communication equipment;
5. Checking the operation of watertight doors, fire doors, fire dampers and main inlets and outlets of ventilating systems in the drill area; and,
6. Checking the necessary arrangements for subsequent abandoning of the ship. (SOLAS III/19.3.4.2)

question:

<Check point>

<Annotation>
The following tests should be carried out:
Daily   · Function of DSC facilities (VHF, MF and HF) using built-in test functions · Battery supplies to GMDSS equipment including charging condition and battery voltage checks.
Weekly
· Function of DSC facilities by way of a test call with a coastal station (if in range or at the earliest opportunity if out of range) · Reserve power supplies to GMDSS equipment other than batteries (e.g. emergency generator)
Monthly · Enhanced group calling (EGC) function · EPIRB function (using built-in test) and condition · SART function (using built-in test) and condition
· Condition and security of batteries · Condition of aerials and insulators · Function test of survival craft two-way VHF equipment (BPG 5th Edition 3.15.6)  Where a reserve source of energy consists of rechargeable accumulator batteries, their capacity shall be checked, using an appropriate method, at intervals not exceeding 12 months, when the ship is not at sea. question:

Are ships personnel aware of the requirements of MARPOL Annex V with respect to the disposal of operational waste and cargo residues from ships?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check garbage record book and GMP.
 - Operational waste mean all solid waste(including slurries) not covered by other Annexes that are collected on board during normal maintenance or operation of a ship or used for cargo stowage and handling.
 - Operational waste also includes cleaning agents and additives contained in cargo holds and external wash water.
 - Operational wastes does not include grey water, bilge water, or other similar discharge essential to the operation of as ship, taking into account the guideline developed by the Organisation.
 - Cargo residues means the remnants of any cargo which are not covered by other Annexes and which remain on the deck or in holds following loading and unloading, including loading and unloading excess or spillage, whether in wet or dry condition or entrained in wash water, but does not include cargo dust remaining on the deck after sweeping or dust on the external surface of the ship.

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Fire Fighting Equipment)
Are CO2 portable fire extinguisher placed near Emergency Switchboards in good order with operating instructions clearly marked and are crew members familiar with their operation?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check fire extinguisher.
Monthly inspection record shall be available.
Portable fire extinguisher shall be near the entrance of service space.
<Annotation>
Each extinguisher should be clearly marked with the following minimum information:
1. Name of the manufacturer;
2. Type of fire for which the extinguisher is suitable;
3. Type and quantity of extinguishing medium;
4. Approval details;
5. Instructions for use and recharge (it is recommended that operating instructions be given in pictorial form);
6. Year of manufacture;
7. Temperature range over which the extinguisher will operate satisfactorily; and
8. Test pressure. (FSS Code 4 and Res. A.951)
One of the portable fire extinguishers intended for use in any space shall be stowed near the entrance to that space. (SOLAS 2004 II- 2/10.3.2.2)
For vessels constructed after 1st July 2002, spare charges shall be provided for 100% of the first ten extinguishers and 50% of the remaining fire extinguishers capable of being recharged on board. Not more than sixty total spare charges are required. Instructions for recharging shall be carried on board. (SOLAS 2004 II-2/10.3.3.1)
For fire extinguishers which cannot be recharged on board, additional portable fire extinguishers of the same quantity, type, capacity and number shall be provided in lieu of spare charges. (SOLAS 2004 II-2/10.3.3.2)
For vessels constructed before 1st July 2002, spare charges shall be provided in accordance with requirements specified by the Administration. (SOLAS 1974 II-2/6.2)
Note: Portable fire extinguishers must be hydrostatically tested every 10 years or lesser period if so required by the Administration. The date of the hydrostatic test must be stamped on the cylinder.

question:

Are lifeboats and rescue boat, including their equipment and launching mechanisms, in good order and have they been launched and maneuvered in the water in accordance with SOLAS requirements?

<Annotation>
<Additional requirement for free-fall launching type lifeboat>
At intervals of not more than six months, the lifeboat shall either be launched by free fall with only the operating crew on board, or simulated launching shall be carried out in accordance with the guidelines developed by the Organization.
<Additional requirement for dedicated rescue boat>
In case the vessel having dedicated rescue boats, rescue boats launching and maneuvering, with assigned crew members, and training on emergency operation, shall be basically done every month (if not practicable at some occasion the interval, however shall not exceed 3 months).

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Life-Saving Apparatus)
<Applicable for davit-launched type lifeboat only>
Is FPD (Fall Preventer Device) used on the occasion of lowering lifeboat? Is there any procedure for using FPD?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check if the FPD is actually used or not by interviewing.
Check if there is any procedure in the SMS manual or Work instruction etc.
If FPD is not used for lowering lifeboat;
- Check the Manufacturer/Type of LRRS, then refer attached "LRRS List".
- In case of following (1) or (2), usage of FPD is not required by IMO circular, however, NYK strongly recommend to use it.
(1) If it is "Compliant" or Newly built vessel after 2013/01/01
(2) If it is "Compliant after modification", and if "Statement of acceptance of the instauration of replacement release and retrieval system to an existing lifeboat) is available onboard.
If it is "non-compliant" or not listed on the attached "LRRS list", the LRRS should be replaced by 1st dry docking after 2014/07/01. Until then, FPD should be used.
If FPD is not used, it should be noted in the observation report with following information.
- type/model of LRRS
- Status of compliance(Compliant/Compliant after modification/Non-compliant/Not Listed)
- If FPD is available on board or not

question:
Deck Management (Hull & Structure)

guideline:
<Check point>

<Annotation>
In the event of accidental or other exceptional discharge of oil, a statement shall be made in the Oil Record Book Part II of the circumstances of, and the reasons for, the discharge. (Oil Record Books Introduction Parts I and II).
Note: The hull should be free from oil staining, extensive coating breakdown or excessive marine growth. Record in comments approximate percentage coating breakdown or areas of marine growth. The hull may be oil stained by passing through an area of oil and not be recorded in the Oil record book. If the hull is stained in this way, record of passing through oil areas should be recorded in the deck log book if such transit occurred during daylight hours.

question:
Deck Management (Hull & Structure)
If a helicopter landing or winching area is provided, does it meet ICS guidelines and, is there a safe access from the hatch cover to deck?
guideline:
<Check point>  As per ICS guide,
Landing area shall not have any obstructions higher than 15cms. Documentary evidence of structural strength shall be on board.
Markings shall be clear and well maintained including obstacles in within landing or winching area.. Winching area shall be properly marked.
FFE for Helicopter operations shall be maintained as per ICS guide or local regulation, whichever is more strict Check:
1) Landing area mark- Mark H:  4.0m×3.0m×(0.75m wide)1m wide yellow touchdown/positioning marking circle
2) Winching area mark- Mark WINCH ONLY with ● minimum diameter more than 5m, 0.3m wide-broken yellow line with mark to space ratio of approximately 4:1
The access from hatch cover to deck should be a fixed height inclined ladder with fixed hand rails and front platform with operational load for two persons (150 KG). The steps and platforms should be made of non-slip materials.
ksm_sms_ref:
ICS Guide to Helicopter/ Ship Operations 4th Ed.
Ch. 4
Rightship 5.44

question:

guideline:
<Check point> Check markings.
If multiple load lines are assigned, only the latest valid load line should be marked. Suggest draft mark soon be repainted unless clearly sighted.
<Annotation>
The permanent marking shall be plainly visible, clear of any other markings on the hull and shall be painted in a contrasting colour. (SOLAS XI-1/3.5.1)
The permanent marking referred to in paragraph 1 shall be not less than 200 mm in height. The permanent marking referred to in paragraph 2 shall be not less than 100 mm in height. The width of the marks shall be proportionate to the height. (SOLAS XI-1/3.5.2)

question:
Deck Management (Hull & Structure)

guideline:
<Check point> Check markings.
<Annotation>
The ship’s identification number shall be permanently marked:
- In a visible place either on the stern of the ship or on either side of the hull, amidships port and starboard, above the deepest assigned load line or either side of the superstructure, port and starboard or on the front of the superstructure; and,
- In an easily accessible place either on one end of the transverse bulkheads of the machinery spaces, or on one of the hatchways or, in the case of tankers, in the pump room. (SOLAS XI-1/3.4)
The permanent marking shall be plainly visible, clear of any other markings on the hull and shall be painted in a contrasting colour. (SOLAS XI-1/3.5.1)
The permanent marking referred to in paragraph 1 shall be not less than 200 mm in height. The permanent marking referred to in paragraph 2 shall be not less than 100 mm in height. The width of the marks shall be proportionate to the height. (SOLAS XI-1/3.5.2) The requirement for the ship’s identification number shall be complied with not later than the first scheduled dry-docking after 1st July 2004 for ships constructed before that date. (SOLAS XI-1/3)

question:
Deck Management (Hull & Structure)
Is the vessel free from any visible bulkhead, valve or pipeline leakage liable to cause pollution?
guideline:
<Check point>
Look for telltale signs of any spill overboard on the shipside.

question:
Deck Management (Hull & Structure)
Is the general condition of service pipework satisfactory and is it free from significant corrosion and pitting and soft patches or other temporary repairs?
guideline:
<Check point>
Any hard rust on hydraulic pipe, hydraulic actuators; fixed fire, foam, DCP (Dry Chemical Powder) line etc. and soft patches or temporary repairs shall be considered as Finding.
<Annotation>
Notes: The following deck pipework should be examined, particularly on the underside, for external indications of corrosion and for patching or accelerated wear caused by rope abrasion:
- Hydraulic and pneumatic pipework;
- Fire mains and associated fittings;
- Deck steam lines;
- Compressed air lines;
- Tank cleaning lines.
Pipe securing arrangements should be intact and permit free movement of the pipes as necessary.

question:
Deck Management (Hull & Structure)
Are pipe stands, clamps, supports and expansion arrangements satisfactory?
guideline:
<Check point>
Visual condition check to be done.

question:
Deck Management (Hull & Structure)
Is the general condition of electrical equipment, including conduits and wiring, satisfactory?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check electric conduits and wiring support.
Check condition of fire retardant cement for maintaining fire boundaries in accommodation.

question:
Deck Management (Hull & Structure)
Are all deck openings, including watertight doors, Bridge windows and portholes, in good order and capable of being properly secured?
guideline:
<Check point> Check lock handle.
Check door/window frames, etc.
Check the condition of rubber packing of watertight doors and portholes. The packing shall be free of any paint and without any gaps. Condition of steel channel housing the rubber packing shall be good. All dogs shall be working efficiently. Note last hydro or chalk test of these doors/ portholes.

question:
Deck Management (Hull & Structure)
Are fuel, ballast and other space vents and air pipes in good order and does visual evidence indicate regular maintenance?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check rust of bonnets. Check operation of floats.
Check condition of open and closing device.
Mark "NO" if there is patch or temporary repair made.
Note: Vent heads should be regularly dismantled to prove that flame screens, where fitted are clean and in good order and that the closing device which prevents the ingress of water is also in good condition and operating correctly.

question:
Deck Management (Hull & Structure)
Are all vents and air pipes clearly marked to indicate the spaces they serve?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check marking on tank vent cover.

question:
Deck Management (Hull & Structure)
Is local valve for FPT kept closed at sea except when ballasting operation is in progress?
Is opening/shutting operation smooth?
guideline:
<Check point> Check local valve.
Check if opening/shutting operation is smooth. Check if valve is kept closed.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Are moorings satisfactorily deployed and tended?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check mooring condition.
Mooring lines of same material and strength shall be deployed. All lines for each lead shall bear similar tension.
<Annotation>
Mooring lines of the same size and type (material) should be used for all leads. Mooring lines should be arranged so that all lines in the same service are about the same length between the ship and the shore bollard.
Note: It is recommended that the entire area of the mooring deck is considered an area of elevated risk, particularly from snap-back, and that personnel are made aware when they are entering this elevated risk area.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Are all mooring lines correctly reeled on drums, secured on brakes and winches out of gear?
guideline:
<Check point> Verify following
1. Pay out direction should be marked as per manufacturers design;
2. Winch shall not be left in gear while on brake under tension
<Annotation>
A band brake is designed to work in one direction only, so the line must always be reeled correctly onto the drum. Each arrangement should be assessed on a case-by-case basis with reference to the manufacturer’s guidance. With lines correctly reeled, tension on the line should be in a direction that causes the free end of the band to be forced towards the fixed end, thereby forcing the two halves of the band together. (MEG 6.3.4.2)
Winches should never be left in gear with the mooring winch band brake on. Hydraulic or electric drives can suffer severe damage should the brake render. Mooring drums should always be left disconnected from the winch drive whenever the mooring line is tensioned and the band brake is fully applied.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Are mooring wires, ropes and synthetic tails and connecting apparatus in good order?
guideline:
<Check point>
There shall be a system of periodic inspection of mooring wires, HMPE ropes and synthetic ropes and synthetic tails. Periodic lubrication of mooring wires shall be in place.
Splicing reduces the SWL by 10%. Minimum 5 tucks shall be allowed for splicing. Eyes of mooring ropes created by knots, e.g. Bowline knot are not acceptable.
<Annotation>
Notes: Splicing of ropes is acceptable, but reduces the strength of the rope by about 10%. Splices in eyes and for repairs should have a minimum of 5 tucks.
Particular attention should be paid to the eyes of mooring wires. If there are more than three broken wires in any strand, or five in any adjacent strands in a length of wire 10 times the diameter, the damaged part requires removal and the wire re-splicing.
There should be a routine for the maintenance of wires and the lubrication of them using a preservative which will effectively penetrate the strands and wires.
(for tankers)
All splices and repairs should be made in strict accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions and performed by a competent person. Records should be maintained of inspections and repairs for each line or tail.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Are rat guards set on mooring lines in good order?
guideline: <Check point> Check rat guards.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Are pedestal fairleads, roller fairleads and other rollers well-greased and free to turn and are bitts and chocks free of grooving?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check by actually moving and external appearance.
Confirm pedestal fairleads, roller fairleads and other rollers are well greased and free to turn.
There shall be a system of periodic inspection and lubrication of pedestal rollers, roller fairleads and other rollers. There shall be no grooving on bitts and chocks.
The surface of bitts, chocks, rollers and mooring drums shall be smooth for deployment of HMPE ropes.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Are mooring winches, including winch foundations in good order?
guideline:
<Check point>
Verify that foundation and winch(s) are in good condition. Check oil leakage and condition of sight glass.
Check rust condition of winch beds and joining sections to deck.
Check each part of mooring equipment (including reduction gear) greased up is enough.
If mooring winches are electrically powered, are insulation tests carried out and the results recorded.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Do brake linings, drums and pins appear to be in good order?
Is there a procedure for testing the winch brake rendering setting and is it being tested regularly?
Is brake rendering point available on the brake screw lever?
guideline:
<Check point>
Look for wear and tear of brake lining, hinge pins and condition of winch drums
<Annotation>
Notes: Defective brake gear is often evident, particularly on older vessels. Check the condition of cheek plates for wastage and distortion, the hinge pins and their retaining devices and the condition of the brake drum below the lining.
If there is significant wear on the brake linings, the brake adjustment screw may be at the limit of its travel and further tightening not possible.
Specific procedures for testing winch brakes should be made available on board.
Mooring winch brakes should be tested in accordance with winch brake manufacturer’s or ship-builder’s guidance or following repair or modification of associated parts.
Check if tests are conducted at least annually for all tankers (recommended by Rightship, BHP).
• The designed maximum heaving load of mooring winch motors, rendering capacity of winch brakes and direction of heave and lowering should be clearly marked on the mooring winch.
• The torque that is to be applied to the hand wheel or handle of the brake should be clearly marked on the winch.
•  Records of winch brake testing, including the torque required to achieve the correct rendering load should be maintained on board.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Are windlasses, anchors, locking bars and cables in good order and operating effectively?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check that locking bar can be properly set to avoid full load of anchor chain on the brake. Check that each part of windlass equipment (including reduction gear) is greased up enough.
<Annotation>
Note: The condition of the locking bars should be checked to ascertain that they function correctly by locking the chain when the vessel is at anchor to prevent the brake having to take the full load of the cable.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Are clutch lever pins of windlasses/mooring winches in place?
guideline: <Check point> Check pins.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Are mooring lines secured to bitts and turned up correctly?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check mooring condition. Verify following
1. one or two full turns on leading post of bitt prior 'figure of eight';
2. mooring rope is not made fast on warping drum;
<Annotation>
The recommended method of turning up a rope on bitts is to take one or two full turns around the leading post before figure of eight. The reason for this is to reduce the tendency to pull the two posts together. However when turning up unjacketed high modulus lines around bitts, for example when a tug’s line fast, two turns should be taken around the leading post prior to turning the line up in a figure of eight fashion (MEG 7.3.2)
Note: Mooring lines must not be secured to winch warping drums.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Are all mooring lines stowed neatly to minimize tripping hazards and are mooring areas clear and unobstructed?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check mooring condition.
Mooring station shall be squared up of mooring lines, heaving lines, messengers etc. after mooring.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
On split drum winches, have the split drums been set up correctly after completion of mooring operation?
guideline:
<Check point>
• Split drum winches are designed so that the line under tension is on the first wrap on the drum providing maximum holding power. Excessive turns should not be left on the working side of a split mooring winch (tension drum). -
If guidance is not available, a minimum of eight turns should be used (Rightship accept minimum 3 turns). Recommend to use bight protector on stowage side.
The rated holding capacity is only achieved with one layer of line on the tension section of the drum. Operation with additional layers will decrease the brake holding capacity.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Is the crew aware of the design limitations of their anchor windlass and systems?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check crew should be familiar with all manufacturer equipment and operation manuals and understand the design/operating limitations of windlasses fitted.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Is mooring equipment marked with its SWL?
guideline:
<Check point>
All bitts, chocks, fairleads shall be permanently marked with SWL.
The SWL of the fitting should be equal to or greater than the ship design MBL. (MEG 1.4.2)
<Annotation>
Each fitting should be clearly marked by bead weld outline with its SWL, in addition to any markings required by other applicable standards. The SWL should be expressed in tonnes (letter ‘t’) and be located so that it is not obscured during the operation of the fitting. It will not be the resultant load on the fitting which may be higher. (MEG 1.4.2)
Note: Some vessels have the mooring equipment marked in 'kN', which is an acceptable alternative.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-2)
Is a gangway provided?
guideline:
<Check point> Check condition.
Gangways should not be used at an angle of inclination greater than 30° from the horizontal and accommodation ladders should not be used at an angle greater than 55° from the horizontal, unless designed and constructed for use at angles greater than the above.
Gangways should never be secured to a ship’s guardrails unless they have been designed for that purpose. If positioned through an open section of bulwark or railings, any remaining gaps should be adequately fenced.
A safety net should be mounted beneath accommodation ladders and gangways where it is possible that a person may fall from the means of embarkation and disembarkation or between the ship and quayside.
Check condition of the handrail.
Check safety lines installed between the handrails, and not slack.
<Annotation>
Any gap between the dockside and the ship, whereby a person on the ship's means of access might fall into the water, should be protected by a safety net, of suitable size, mesh and construction, secured to the ship and dockside, as appropriate.
When using additional wharf short ladder, a proper Risk Assessment be made when using such means of access where the inspection and testing regime is unknown.
A ship’s gangway consists of a straight, lightweight bridging structure provided with side stanchions and handrails. The walking surface has a non-slip surface or transverse bars to provide foot grips for when it is inclined. It is rigged perpendicular to the ship's side and spans between the ship's rail and the working deck of the berth. (ISGOTT 16.4.3.2)
regulation_ref:
MSC.1/Circ. 1331,
Guidelines for Constructio n, Installation, Maintenanc e and Inspection/S urvey of Means of Embarkatio n and Disembarka tion, 2009

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-2)
Are accommodation ladders, gangways, pilot ladders where fitted, maintained in good condition and inspected regularly?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check corrosion of platforms, and bends of handrails/ platforms. Check condition of Hoisting Wire
Check standard of Hoisting Wire replacement Check inspection and maintenance record
For vessels constructed on or after July 01 2012, there shall be Certificate showing that Pilot ladder is compliant with IMO Resln 1045(27).  It is not applicable for vessels constructed before July 01 2012 (only recommended as reasonably as practicable).
Check if SWL and the permissible numbers of person are displayed on the gang way.
Accommodation ladder or gangway should be clearly marked at each end with a plate showing maximum number of persons allowed at one time, maximum and minimum permitted design angles of inclination, design load, maximum load on bottom end plate, etc.
<Annotation>
All wires used to support the means of embarkation and disembarkation shall be maintained and inspected with special regard to the areas passing through sheaves. The falls should be ‘renewed when necessary due to the deterioration of the falls or at intervals of not more than five years, whichever is the earlier as per SOLAS III/20.4, SOLAS II-1/3- and MSC.1/Circ.1206.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-2)
Are Pilot boarding and access arrangements satisfactory?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check visually external appearance.
Check steps, spreaders, manropes, marine ropes, etc. If combination arrangement is used then
Combination ladder shall be in compliance with IMO MSC.1/Circ.1428.
Check if Pilot transfer arrangement poster is in compliance with  MSC.1/Circ.1428.

question:
Deck Management (Accommodation & Stores)
Are all loose gear on deck, in stores and in internal spaces properly secured and maintained?
guideline:
<Check point> Check condition.
All loose gear, pipes, drums etc. shall not be secured with pipework e.g. drain pipes etc.
Check SPM E 448 Loose Gear Inspection Record

question:
Deck Management (Accommodation & Stores)
Are the chain locker doors securely battened down?
guideline: <Check point> Check condition.

question:
Deck Management (Accommodation & Stores)
Is the general condition of service pipework on deck including Bosun Store satisfactory and is it free from significant corrosion and pitting and soft patches or other temporary repairs?
guideline:
<Check point> Check condition.
Any hard rust on hydraulic pipe, hydraulic actuators; fixed fire, foam, DCP line etc. AND soft patches or temporary repairs shall be considered as Finding.
<Annotation>
Notes: The following deck pipework should be examined, particularly on the underside, for external indications of corrosion and for patching or accelerated wear caused by rope abrasion:
- Hydraulic and pneumatic pipework;
- Fire mains and associated fittings;
- Deck steam lines;
- Compressed air lines;
- Tank cleaning lines.
Pipe securing arrangements should be intact and permit free movement of the pipes as necessary.

question:
Deck Management (Accommodation & Stores)
Is the forecastle space free of water, internal spaces and storerooms clean, free from debris and tidy?
guideline:
<Check point> Check condition.
Check Water tightness, tidiness and cleanliness, leak from hydraulic equipment, etc. Check Rubber packing for openings.
Verify that warning is posted near bilge discharge valve against accidental oily water mixture discharge.
If fitted, test the bilge high level alarm. Check record.

question:
Deck Management (Accommodation & Stores)
Have heaving lines been constructed with a monkey’s fist at one end free of any added weighting material?
guideline:
<Check point>
• Check the  “monkey’s fist” should be made with rope only and must not contain added weighting material.
<Annotation>
Safe alternatives include a small high-visibility soft pouch, filled with fast-draining pea shingle or similar, with a weight of not more than 0.5 kg. Under no circumstances is a line to be weighted by items such as shackles, bolts or nuts, or twist locks.
ksm_sms_ref:
Code of
Safe Working Practices for Merchant Seafarer’s, 2017

question:
Deck Management (Others)
Are light fittings in gas-hazardous areas Ex 'd' rated and in good order? (Battery Room, Paint Store, and other gas hazardous areas)
guideline:
<Annotation>
Notes: Lights will be either explosion-proof or pressurized. The flame paths of explosion-proof lights should not be painted over. Fluorescent fittings will generally have flame paths at each end.
The manufacturer’s or Administration’s certificate approving the fitting for use in gas-hazardous areas will be invalidated if the correct bolts for securing the cover, or the correct light bulb size, are not used.
Particular attention should be paid to the following:
- Cracks in metal, cracked or broken glasses or failure of cement around cemented glasses in flameproof or explosion proof enclosures;
- Covers of flameproof enclosures to ensure that they are tight, that no bolts are missing, and that no gaskets are present between mating metal surfaces;
- Each connection to ensure that it is properly connected;
- Possible slackness of joints in conduit runs and fittings;
Vent fan, cargo pump and cargo winch motors and lighting are likely to be found within gas-hazardous areas. An Ex‘d’ rating means that the equipment can withstand an internal explosion without igniting the outside atmosphere. Ex ‘e’ is an increased safety rating.

question:
Machinery Management (Electrical Equipment)
Are the deck and accommodation lights all operational and sufficient in number and range to illuminate the deck to facilitate safe working during darkness?
guideline:
<Check point> Check deck lights.
Verify that all deck lights are properly trimmed and in good working condition
<Annotation>
Notes: The level of deck lighting should be adequate to allow:
- Sufficient visibility to permit safe access to all areas of the deck
- The safe use of mooring equipment;
- The monitoring of the deck area for spills and leakages;
- The monitoring of all deck areas and the adjacent surrounding areas to prevent unauthorized access.

question:
Cargo & Ballast Management (Dry Cargo Common)
Is the cargo crane machinery including controls in the operator’s cabin, inspected, tested and maintained as per manufacturer’s recommendations and PMS?
guideline:
<Check point>
1. Crane cabs should not have a paint smell.
2. The crane cab should be clean (free from apparent leak, trash and grease). 3. Crane seats should be in good condition (wobbly chairs are not allowed).
4. Crane windows should be clean (free of grease, paint, and condensation). 5. All wipers on windows should be in working condition.
6. If no heavy corrosion of Crane Operator’s Cabin including the Floor, cabin bolts, etc.; 7. Check PMS
7. Check SPM E 419 CRANE MAINTENANCE CHECKLIST is being utilized.
8. Check BGCM S 204 Vessel Crane Inspection checklist

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Fire Fighting Equipment)
Are fire mains, pumps, hoses and nozzles in good order and available for immediate use?
guideline:
<Check point>
Visual condition check to be done. Check patch, double, etc.
Check leak from fire hydrants.
PSC will not accept any temporary repair.

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Fire Fighting Equipment)
<Applicable vessel only>
Is vessel provided with firefighting equipment for helicopter operations? Is firefighting equipment for helicopter operations in good order?
Are the fire hose laid, connected and charged with water?
Are the foam hoses length enough to reach from the hydrant to helicopter working area?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check if vessel is provided with:
Dry powder - 1 or 2 extinguisher with total capacity of not less than 45kg
CO2 - 1 or 2 extinguisher with total capacity of not less than 18kg (Refer - Class NK TEC0762) Foam System - as per chapter 4.7 of ICS
Fire hoses - at least 2 nozzle with dual purpose type (jet / spray) Fireman's outfit - 2 complete outfit
Emergency tools - red emergency signalling lamp, large axe, crowbar, adjustable wrench, fire resistant blanket, 60cm bolt/wire cutters, grab or salving hook, heavy duty hacksaw (w/ 6 spare blades), ladder, fireline 5mmdia. x 15m in length, side cutting pliers, set of assorted screwdrivers, harnesss knife complete with sheath and first aid kit.
It is not necessary to store all these in one place.

to Helicopter/S hip Operations 4.7

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Fire Fighting Equipment)
Are fire flaps on fan room and cargo hold ducts clearly marked to indicate the spaces they serve and can readily be closed in good order?
guideline:
<Check point> Check markings.
Check numbering or naming.
Check condition of fan room, fan casing, wire net, etc.
Dampers are clearly marked for easy opening/closing operations.
If possible, check flap/lid of damper and confirm it is not heavily damaged by corrosion.

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Fire Fighting Equipment)
Are the crew familiar with the fixed and portable fire extinguishing systems, where fitted, in good order and are clear operating instructions posted?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check to see if portable fire extinguishers are placed outside.
Pictographic operating instructions for fixed fire fighting systems, where fitted. All valves clearly marked. Check that nozzles of water spray system in Paint locker are not blocked with pale of paint/ thinner.
<Additional check point for Japanese and Panamanian Flag Vessels only> Provision of any of foam, CO2 or dry chemical extinguishers.
*If water-spraying systems approved by flag state are provided, no portable fire extinguishers are required.
<Additional check point for Liberian Flag Vessels only>
1) New vessels built in and after February 1992 -
For floor area of less than 10 ㎡:  either 1 portable fire extinguisher of CO2 gas of 6.8 kg or 1 dry chemical extinguisher of 4.5 kg.
For floor area of more than10 ㎡:  Any of fixed fire extinguishing system of CO2, dry chemical system or water- spraying system operable from outside.
2) Existing vessels - 10 ㎡ above reads 20 ㎡.

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Fire Fighting Equipment)
Is flame arrester/screen of vent opening in good order?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check to see if flame arrester is removed or broken.

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Fire Fighting Equipment)
Are the crew familiar with the CO2 cylinder or tank fixed fire extinguishing systems, where fitted, and is in good order and are clear operating instructions posted?
guideline:
<Check point>
Pictographic operating instructions for fixed fire fighting systems, where fitted. All valves clearly marked. Check to see if actuating box is unhooked in vibrations.
If one tank type, check condition of refrigeration unit and tank level. Check pressure of starting bottle, if possible.
Check general condition of CO2 cylinder/tank. Check general condition of room inside.
Note this room is not used as storeroom.
Check if blown through with compressed air and checked to ensure they are free of dust and debris.

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Fire Fighting Equipment)
Is key to box for releasing CO2 managed properly?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check who manages key and where key is kept. Mark "N/A" if key is not provided for box.

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Fire Fighting Equipment)
Are records available to show that samples of foam compound have been tested at regular intervals?
guideline:
<Check point>
For fixed foam fire fighting system, foam concentrate shall be initially tested after 3years of delivery then after every year. Original and valid Foam test Certificate shall be on board.
<Annotation>
Protein based alcohol foam concentrates should be subject to a stability test with Acetone.
Except for tests above, the first periodical control of foam concentrates should be performed not more than 3 years after being supplied to the ship, and after that, every year. The tests required above should be performed prior to delivery to the ship and annual thereafter. (MSC.1/Circ 1312).

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Fire Fighting Equipment)
Are the crew familiar with foam fixed fire extinguishing systems, where fitted, in good order and are clear operating instructions posted?
guideline:
<Check point>
Pictographic operating instructions for fixed fire fighting systems, where fitted. All valves clearly marked. Check liquid level in storage tank.
Check leaks.
Check general condition of room inside. Note this room is not used as storeroom.

question:
Emergency Preparedness (Fire Fighting Equipment)
Are the crew familiar with Hypermist fixed fire extinguishing systems, where fitted, in good order and are clear operating instructions posted?
Is there a minimum test of one section in each open head water mist system by flowing water through the nozzles?
<The sections tested should be chosen so that all sections are tested within a five-year period>
guideline:
<Check point>
Pictographic operating instructions for fixed fire fighting systems, where fitted. All valves clearly marked. Check that Hypermist system is on "AUTO" mode and that water inlet valve is kept OPEN at all times.
Check the control panel and confirm the changeover switch is kept turned ON.(Sometimes it is kept turned OFF intentionally) Check if fire detectors for automatic start are not isolated/disabled.
Check by interviewing and confirm the officers know how to use it
Check water supply valve and confirm it is OPEN.(Sometimes it is kept CLOSED intentionally) Check liquid level in storage tank, if fitted, and check leaks.
Check quality of water as per manufacturer's guideline (if fitted with dedicated tank).

question:
Pollution Prevention (Oil Pollution Prevention)
Are means readily available for dealing with small oil or chemical spills?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check the inventory of Oil Spill containment equipment in SOPEP or SMPEP. Enquire the reason, if there is any reduction in oil dispersant chemical.
Check if materials/equipment are ready for use during cargo work or bunkering. Check storage place of solvent and dispersant.
Check record of quantity of materials/equipment.

question:
Pollution Prevention (Oil Pollution Prevention)
Are unused cargo and/or bunker pipeline manifolds fully bolted and are all drains and vents and unused gauge stems, suitably blanked or capped?
guideline:
<Check point>
Bunker and cargo manifolds, gauge and temperature stems, drains and vents shall be blanked or capped. Bolts should be of sufficient length and all nuts to be fully screwed.

question:
Pollution Prevention (Oil Pollution Prevention)
Is the ship fitted with a main deck boundary coaming and scupper arrangement that is effectively plugged during operations?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check all deck scuppers.
Vessels engaged in bunkering are required to have all deck scuppers plugged

question:
Pollution Prevention (Oil Pollution Prevention)
Are bunker pipelines been satisfactorily tested atleast annual  basis and is there suitable evidence of this test?
guideline:
<Check point> Check record
Pipe lines shall be stenciled with date of test and value of pressure test.
- The frequency of the tests and inspections required by this section must be annually or as part of the biennial and mid-period inspections.
Bunker pipe lines shall be pressure tested to
1. 100%MAWP (max. allowable working pressure) annually. Compressed Air shall not be used as means of pressure testing.
2. 150%MAWP during each scheduled dry docking

question:
Pollution Prevention (Bilge)
Are the overboard valve and intermediate valves properly closed after discharging hold bilge?
guideline: <Check point> Confirm by Interview

question:
Safety Management (Safety Culture)
Are all movable objects on deck or in each storeroom properly secured?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check movable objects.
Check free from debris and tidy.

question:
Safety Management (Safety Culture)
Are paints stored in specified place?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check if paints are stored in Bosun's Store, Steering Gear compartment, or Engine Room workshop. Check by interviewing deck crew where paints are stored.
Check also how paint cans are secured. Paints must be stored only in specified place. Check MSDS available.

question:
Safety Management (Work Environment)
Is gas welding and burning equipment in good order ?
guideline:

Non-return valves must be checked to ensure they are fully operational. Overhaul of non-return valves at regular intervals should be incorporated into the planned maintenance system. Inspection and testing of these non-return valves should be incorporated in the pre- loading checks of the holds. question:
Deck Management (Hull & Structure)
Are water ingress detector and alarm system (WIAS) maintained in good condition and are the records of tests being maintained?
guideline:
<Check point>
Check maintenance and condition of WIAS
<Annotation>
• In each cargo hold, giving audible and visual alarms, one when the water level above the inner bottom in any hold reaches a height of 0.5m and another at a height not less than 15% of the depth of the cargo hold but not more than 2.0 m. On bulk carriers to which regulation 9.2 applies, only the latter alarm need be installed. The water level detectors shall be fitted in the aft end of the cargo holds. For cargo holds which are used for water ballast, an alarm overriding device may be installed. The visual alarms shall clearly discriminate between the two different level detectors in each hold;
• In any ballast tank forward of the collision bulkhead required by regulation II-1/11, giving an audible and visual alarm when the liquid in the tank reaches a level not exceeding 10% of the tank capacity. An alarm overriding device may be installed to be activated when the tank is in use; and
• In any dry or void space other than a chain cable locker, any part of which extends forward of the foremost cargo hold, giving an audible and visual alarm at a water level of 0.1 m above the deck. Such alarms need not be provided in enclosed spaces the volume of which does not exceed 0.1% of the ship’s maximum displacement volume.
• The audible and visual alarms specified in paragraph 1 shall be located on the navigation bridge. The record of testing of alarm systems should be retained on board.

question:
Cargo & Ballast Management (Bulk-Common)
Is following countermeasure to prevent serious damage of bulkhead by ballasting?
1. Chief officer must understand the limitations of port use ballast tanks through the loading manual.
2. Chief officer must make a cargo-loading plan that includes the ballast operation and identity limitation of port use ballast hold, if have.
3. The company must provide the procedure / Work Instruction for ballasting/de-ballasting operation, including the following measures of limitation of hold ballasting.
- A permissible water level and caution mark should be displayed as plainly on all port-use ballast holds (cargo hold BHD and hatch cover air-vent).
- A sounding height of a permissible level and caution mark should be displayed as plainly on all sounding points for port-use ballast holds.
- A permissible water level and caution should be displayed as plainly at a suitable place on the ballast console or Ship's office.
- A notice indication – a comprehensible rough sketch of the permissible water level for each port-use ballast hold – should be displayed in the ship’s office.
4. Carry out adequate and frequent soundings, especially when the level
comes close to planned limits.
5. Establish immediate communication between the ballast-pump station, local valve and the sounding crew on site.

question:
Deck Management (Deck Machinery-1)
Is there a procedure to ensure monitoring the damage, evaluation and protection of mooring ropes?
Are ropes rinsed with fresh water after each port operation to remove cargo and salt deposits, cover with hard / thick canvas to minimise sun / sea spray exposure, protect chafing portions of mooring ropes?
guideline:
<Check point>
• Check regular inspection and protection of mooring lines in accordance with manufacturer’s recommendation and the (PMS)
• Check if adequate spare mooring lines are on board.
• Check during monitoring and adjusting mooring lines whilst a vessel is alongside in tidal ports (Ex: Port Headland) if Masters and watch keepers undertake dynamic risk assessment after considering each of the following factors, but not limited to:
1. Strengths and limitations of each rope (type, MBL, end to end turn date, any visible minor damages / abrasions, prior experience).
2. Strengths and limitations of each winch (brake rendering capacity, condition of brake lining, overall performance of winch and hydraulic system, prior experience).
3. Understanding of tidal effect on the vessel.
4. Understanding bow cushion / bank suction effect caused by passing vessels at close proximity.
5. Understanding the consequence of mooring line failure – vessel moving away from the berth and potentially grounding just outside berth pocket.
6. Understanding the impact if a wire or rope contacts 50% of the circumference of a fairlead or roller and lead through an excessive angle.
7. Other safety related considerations as per your company SMS.

question:
Cargo & Ballast Management (Dry Cargo Common)
Are the stresses, stability information and any limitations included in the cargo plan, understood by the cargo watch officers and are conditions being monitored and maintained within design limits throughout the cargo operation?
guideline:
<Check point>
• The cargo operation and intended ballast/de-ballast procedure are synchronised.
• Draught surveys are conducted at appropriate steps of the loading/discharge plan to verify the ship's condition.
• The draught readings, usually taken at amidships and the fore and aft perpendiculars, should be in good agreement with values calculated in the loading/discharging plan.
• Ballast tanks are sounded to verify their contents and rate of ballasting/de-ballasting.
• The cargo load is in agreement with the figures provided by the terminal.
• The SWSF, SWBM and, where appropriate, hold cargo weight versus draught calculations are performed at intermediate stages of the cargo operation. These results should be logged.
• Any revised loading/unloading plan should be signed by a terminal representative and by the master or chief officer.
• The master and chief officer should be aware of the worst case damage condition for the existing cargo on board.

question:
Cargo & Ballast Management (Bulk-Common)
Has the Master been provided with a signed certificate or declaration, indicating the moisture content, transportable moisture limit (TML), flow moisture limit (FML) and density?
guideline:
<Check point>
Before loading is started copies of all appropriates certificates for the cargo shall be provided, for example moisture content, transportable moisture limit (TML) and density.
<Annotation>
(For loading coal cargo)
Coal shall be classified as Group A and B unless classified as Group B only by a test determined by appropriate authority or where it has the following particle size distribution:
1. not more than 10 % by weight of particles less than 1 mm (D10>1mm) ;and 2. not more than 50 % by weight of particles less than 10 mm (D50>10mm).
For Shippers Declaration, confirm the following:
(a) When loading coal is classified as “Group A and B” on cargo declaration Vessel shall check the following:
① Certificate of transportable moisture limit (TML certificate),
② Certificate of approval for the procedures for sampling, testing, and controlling the moisture content for solid bulk cargo that may liquefy (4.4.3 of the IMSBC Code)
③ Certificate of moisture content
(b) When loading coal is classified as “Group B”
Vessel shall check whether a declaration has a description of a testing as evidence of Group B cargo by appropriate authority OR particle sizing.

question:

The vessel's Safety Management System should indicate which fields are required to be completed in the engine logbook. Entries should include;
 - Vessels operating UMS, the times when UMS and manned status; - Bunkering operations and major internal oil transfers;
- Fuel and lube oil ROB's;

- Machinery operating parameters (RPM, load, temperature and pressures)

Errors made in the log should be struck through with a single line and initialled and dated. Random sampling of logs should be made to ascertain running hours within maintenance periods, shared hours on generators and alarms identified and not by-passed.

question:
Machinery Management (Engine Room Management)
Are diesel engine high and low pressure fuel delivery pipes adequately jacketed or screened,  exhaust lines and hot surfaces protected from spray and surrounding areas free from fuel or lube oil leakage?
guideline:
<Check point>
Note FO / DO line is in good order.
All high pressure delivery pipes of fuel delivery to engines shall be double jacketed. These pipes shall be in leak free condition.
<Annotation>
External high pressure fuel delivery lines between the high pressure fuel pumps and fuel injectors shall be protected with a jacketed piping system capable of containing fuel from a high pressure line failure. A jacketed pipe incorporates an outer pipe into which the high pressure fuel pipe is placed, forming a permanent assembly. The jacketed piping system shall include a means for collection of leakages and arrangements shall be provided for an alarm to be given of a fuel line failure. (SOLAS II-2/4.2.2.5.2)

<Check point>

<Annotation>
PSC may be detained the vessel under suspicion for illegal bilge discharge at PSC inspection due to misunderstanding such plastic temporally pipe as "Magic pipe".
